'''Friedman's SSCG function''' is a [[mathematical function]] defined by [[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]]. It is defined by <math>\text{SSCG}(k)</math> as the largest integer <math>n</math> satisfying the following:
:There is a sequence <math>G_1,\ldots,G_n</math> of simple subcubic graphs such that each <math>G_i</math> has at most <math>i+k</math> vertices and for no <math>i < j</math> is <math>G_i</math> [[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|homeomorphically]] embeddable into <math>G_j</math>.

Later, Friedman defined the more general subcubic graphs <math>\text{SCG}(k)</math>.

== Background ==
In [[mathematics]], especially [[graph theory]], a '''simple subcubic graph''' ('''SSCG''') is a finite simple [[Graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] in which each [[vertex (graph theory)|vertex]] has a [[vertex degree|degree]] of at most three. Suppose we have a sequence of simple subcubic graphs <math>G_1</math>, <math>G_2</math>, ... such that each graph <math>G_i</math> has at most <math>i+k</math> vertices (for some integer <math>k</math>) and for no <math>i<j</math> is <math>G_i</math> [[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|homeomorphically embeddable]] into (i.e. is a [[graph minor]] of) <math>G_j</math>.

The [[Robertson–Seymour theorem]] proves that subcubic graphs (simple or not) are well-quasi-ordered by homeomorphic embeddability, implying such a sequence cannot be infinite. Then, by applying [[Kőnig's lemma]] on the tree of such sequences under extension, for each value of <math>k</math> there is a sequence with maximal length. The function <math>\text{SSCG}(k)</math> denotes that length for simple subcubic graphs. The function <math>\text{SCG}(k)</math> denotes that length for (general) subcubic graphs.

[[Harvey Friedman (mathematician)|Harvey Friedman]] defined two functions: SSCG and SCG.

==SSCG function==
[[File:SSCG(3) sequence.png|thumb|upright=1.38|alt=Sequence of subcubic graphs|A sequence of subcubic graphs. The <math>n</math>-th graph in the sequence contains at most <math>n+3</math> vertices, and no graph is homeomorphically embeddable within any later graph in the sequence. <math>\operatorname{SSCG}(3)</math> is defined to be the longest possible length of such a sequence.]]

Friedman defined <math>\text{SSCG}(k)</math> as the largest integer <math>n</math> satisfying the following:<ref name="SSCG">{{cite web |last1=Friedman |first1=Harvey |title=[FOM] 274:Subcubic Graph Numbers |url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-April/010305.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240407194353/https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-April/010305.html |archive-date=7 April 2024}}</ref>

:There is a sequence <math>G_1,\ldots,G_n</math> of simple subcubic graphs such that each <math>G_i</math> has at most <math>i+k</math> vertices and for no <math>i < j</math> is <math>G_i</math> [[Homeomorphism (graph theory)|homeomorphically]] embeddable into <math>G_j</math>.

The first few terms of the sequence are
: <math> \operatorname{SSCG}(0) = 2, </math>
: <math> \operatorname{SSCG}(1) = 5, </math> &nbsp;and
: <math> \operatorname{SSCG}(2) = 3\cdot2^{3\cdot2^{95}}\!\!-8 = 3\cdot2^{118\,842\,243\,771\,396\,506\,390\,315\,925\,504}\! - 8</math>
: <math> \qquad \qquad \; \approx\, 3.241\,704\,229 \cdot 10^{35\,775\,080\,127\,201\,286\,522\,908\,640\,065} </math>
: <math> \qquad \qquad \; \approx\, 10^{3.5775 \,\cdot\, 10^{28}} .</math><ref>{{Cite OEIS |A300403 |2=Smallest integer i such that SSCG(i) >= n.}}</ref>

It has been shown that the next term, <math>\text{SSCG}(3)</math>, is greater than [[TREE(3)]].<ref name="numberphile">{{YouTube|id=4-eXjTH6Mq4|title="Immense Subcubic Graph Numbers - Numberphile"}}</ref> Friedman showed that <math>\text{SSCG}(13)</math> is greater than the halting time of any [[Turing machine]] that can be proved to halt in [[Reverse mathematics#Π11 comprehension Π11-CA0|Π{{su|p=1|b=1}}-CA<sub>0</sub>]] with at most <math>2\uparrow\uparrow2000</math>{{ref label|tetration|a|^ a}} symbols, and that it cannot be proved to exist in that theory with less than <math>2\uparrow\uparrow1000</math> symbols, where <math>\uparrow\uparrow</math> denotes [[tetration]]. He does this using a similar idea as with a similar statement he proved about <math>\text{TREE}(3)</math>.<ref name="SSCG"/>

==SCG function==

Later, Friedman realized there was no good reason for imposing "simple" on subcubic graphs. He relaxes the condition and defines <math>\text{SCG}(k)</math> as the largest <math>n</math> satisfying:<ref>{{cite web |last1=Friedman |first1=Harvey |title=[FOM] 279:Subcubic Graph Numbers/restated |url=https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-April/010362.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240513162729/https://cs.nyu.edu/pipermail/fom/2006-April/010362.html |archive-date=13 May 2024}}</ref>

:There is a sequence <math>G_1,\ldots,G_n</math> of subcubic graphs such that each <math>G_i</math> has at most <math>i+k</math> vertices and for no <math>i < j</math> is <math>G_i</math> homeomorphically embeddable into <math>G_j</math>.

The first term of the sequence is <math>\text{SCG}(0)=6</math>, while the next term <math>\text{SCG}(1)</math> is bigger than [[Graham's number]]. Furthermore, <math>\text{SCG}(3)</math> is bigger than <math>\text{TREE}^{\text{TREE}(3)}(3)</math>.<ref name="numberphile"/>

Adam P. Goucher claims there is no qualitative difference between the asymptotic growth rates of SSCG and SCG. He writes "It's clear that <math>\text{SCG}(n) \ge \text{SSCG}(n)</math>, but I can also prove <math>\text{SSCG}(4n+3) \ge \text{SCG}(n)</math>".<ref>[https://cp4space.wordpress.com/2012/12/19/fast-growing-2/comment-page-1/#comment-1036 TREE(3) and impartial games | Complex Projective 4-Space<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>
